title: Bootstrap fallback matrix & mini-smoke
content:
Purpose:
A compact, practical triage and quick-fix playbook for Private deployments (VPC / on-prem) focused on fast detection, containment and safe fallback during bootstrap and immediate post-upgrade windows. This is intentionally short — use it for 0-30 minute triage and initial rollback decisions.

Scope and intent:
- Covers common install/runtime failures seen in 2024–2025 on customer on-prem clusters and VPC air-gapped installs.
- Blend of Terraform-module checks, runtime service probes, and upgrade-window rollback triggers.
- Not a full postmortem checklist; follow with detailed autopsy doc after the incident is contained.

Quick triage checklist (0–10 minutes):
1) Is the customer reporting CPU/GPU OOM or service unreachable? Ask for the timestamp and the first failing endpoint.
2) Confirm control plane reachable: curl -sS https://<control-plane-ip>:8443/health || check SSH to control-plane host.
3) Check Terraform apply status (if an upgrade just ran): ask for operator console log or run `terraform show -json` on the same state file. If operator not available, ask for last `apply` window timestamp.
4) Gather logs: kube-system pods, runtime daemon logs, and system journal from nodes. Commands to share (ask customer to paste output):
   - kubectl -n redwood get pods -o wide --show-labels
   - kubectl -n redwood describe pod <failing-pod>
   - journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 500 --no-pager | tail -n 200
   - dmesg | tail -n 100

Rapid-scoring for root-cause (probabilities are heuristic):
- Missing/failed TF modules or providers (30%): failed apply or drift leading to missing volumes, CRDs, or service endpoints.
- Image pull / registry auth (15%): common when private registries rotate creds during upgrade.
- Node-level kernel OOM/pci errors (20%): hardware or driver mismatch after kernel update.
- KV cache/connectivity and routing (20%): gRPC/redis failure causing request stall.
- Config/secret mismatch (15%): incorrect KMS/HSM access or env var typo.

Fallback matrix (decision guidance):
- Severity A (service down, customer SLA impacted): If last change was a TF/helm upgrade within the 2-hour window, trigger fallback to previously pinned model runtime image and rollback TF state where possible.
- Severity B (degraded latency/error rates): Attempt config-only rollback (flip feature flags, reduce batch sizes) before full TF rollback.
- Severity C (minor warnings): Continue observation; gather metrics and escalate if trend persists beyond 60 minutes.

Automated pre-check probes (run before any rollback):
- TF drift probe: `terraform plan -var-file=live.tfvars -refresh=false` (look for resource deletions or replacement plans).
- API handshake: `curl -sS https://<control-plane>/v1/ping -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'` expect 200/OK and RTT < 150ms.
- KV health: redis-cli -h <host> PING; check TTL skew on prefix caches.

Terraform module notes (common pitfalls & quick mitigations):
- Provider version pinning: upgrades often break `google`/`aws` providers; if provider plugin missing, `terraform init -upgrade` may help but avoid in-window. Prefer redeploy with previously tagged module commit.
- Stateful resources: PV/PVC and LVG changes can silently cause node evacuations. Check `kubectl get pvc -A` for pending binds and `kubectl describe sc` for changed ReclaimPolicy.
- Drift in networking: changes to route tables, security groups, or BGP sessions can break control plane reachability. Use `terraform state list | grep network` to inspect recent resource changes.
- Module wrapper scripts: some customers wrap modules with local-exec provisioning — those fail more often in air-gapped installs. Ask for wrapper logs in `/var/log/infra-hooks.log`.

Mini-smoke tests (post-fix verification, 5–15 minutes):
1) Control plane health: /v1/ping, /v1/metrics, and /v1/version endpoints.
2) Model runtime basic generate: POST /v1/generate with a 16-token prompt, expect response < 2s (local latency targets vary).
3) KV cache parity: write a small key via control plane and read it back from a runtime node.
4) Inference load sanity: run 5 concurrent short requests and ensure no 500s.

Common error signatures and suggested probes (copy/paste for Slack ticket):
- "OOM killed: oom_reaper" => check node free memory, container memory limits, and `dmesg` for OOM score. If recent kernel update, consider kernel rollback to previous known-good.
- "Failed to create volume" => check CSI driver, PVC events, and storage class parameters. Ask for `kubectl get events -A --field-selector type=Warning`.
- "ImagePullBackOff" => collect `kubectl describe pod`; verify registry credentials and image digest pinned in TF.
- "gRPC: UNAVAILABLE" between control plane and runtime => check BGP/route table, MTU mismatches, and iptables FORWARD policy.

Sample safe commands for operators (non-destructive):
- kubectl -n redwood logs deployment/control-plane --tail=200
- kubectl -n redwood get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 100
- terraform state pull > state.json; grep -n "replace" state.json || true

Rollback triggers (explicit thresholds):
- >50% of model endpoints returning 5xx for 10 minutes => roll back to pinned runtime image version and pause ongoing TF changes.
- Auto-scaling failures (unable to spin nodes after upgrade) => revert node pool image and restore autoscaler config.

Upgrade window plan (recommended short checklist for future runs):
1) Preflight (T-48h): run dry-run with production-like state, run automated smoke suite in staging that mirrors PV/PVC/storage classes.
2) Preflight (T-1h): snapshot Terraform state, record control-plane and runtime image digests, take cluster-level etcd snapshot.
3) Execute (T0): apply infra changes in small batches (one AZ / host group at a time).
4) Post-change (T+5m, T+30m): run mini-smoke tests above. If any check fails, pause and follow fallback matrix.

Communication template (use for customer Slack/email):
- Subject: [ACTION] Deploy issue — control-plane instability — initiating quick mitigation
- Body: Short summary, timestamp, immediate mitigation (e.g., paused rollout, started rollback to image vX.Y), next check at +15 minutes, request for specific logs.

Escalation path and handoff notes:
- If hardware/kernel suspected -> SRE on-call + infra eng (Ravi) + customer host admin.
- If TF or provider plugin suspected -> Eng infra + module owner (Maya).
- If KMS/HSM access issues -> Security + customer infra (Maya + Darren).

Post-containment tasks (follow-up items to convert into incident ticket):
- Full terraform plan/pull diff, timeline of applied changes, and all related logs.
- Reproduce failure in staging with a replay of the same TF plan and module versions.
- If rollback performed, schedule a small-window reattempt that isolates the suspected change.

Notes and heuristics from past incidents:
- Air-gapped installs often hide registry auth errors — always check image digests rather than tags.
- Small wrapper scripts that run as cronjobs during bootstrap cause 40% of PV mount failures we’ve seen.
- When in doubt, prefer application-level rollback (pin/runtime image) over infra-level rollback (state rollback) because it is faster and lower blast radius.

Appendix: quick grep patterns
- Search for OOMs: `journalctl -k | egrep -i "out of memory|oom"`
- Kubernetes volume errors: `kubectl get events --all-namespaces | egrep -i "attach|mount|volume|persistent"`
- GRPC connectivity: `ss -tnp | egrep ":50051|:50052"`

Low-priority TODOs to convert into follow-up docs:
- Automated pre-checker terraform action (CI job) to detect unsafe PV/SC changes.
- Small runbook for customers to collect a standard debugging bundle (logs + state dump + metrics).
- Better telemetry around image-digest drift in private registries.

End of doc.
